facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Male Selkies were said to cause storms and seduce mortal women who cried seven tears into the sea.

facts_and_myths.claim: Selkies were venomous predatory monsters that ate Scottish fishermen.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Selkies are gentle, romantic, and tragic beings who never harm mortals.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The animated film Song of the Sea beautifully depicts Selkie folklore.

name: Kelpie
visual_anchor: Magnificent midnight-black stallion with waterweed tangled in its dripping wet mane, standing invitingly beside the misty shore of a Scottish loch.
core_traits: Shape-shifting aquatic horse spirit haunting the lochs and deep rivers of Scotland
Appears as a magnificent tame horse standing near water to lure weary travelers or children to mount it
Its magical skin becomes instantly adhesive, trapping riders so they cannot dismount
Dives into the deep water to drown and devour its victims, leaving only the entrails on the shore

facts_and_myths.claim: The famous 100-foot-tall horse-head sculptures in Falkirk, Scotland, are named The Kelpies.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sculptor Andy Scott created two colossal steel horse heads named The Kelpies to honor Scotland's horse-powered industrial heritage.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A Kelpie can be tamed and put to work if a mortal manages to capture it with a silver bridle.

facts_and_myths.claim: Kelpies are gentle, winged horses that fly between clouds like Pegasus.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Kelpies have no wings; they are predatory freshwater monsters associated with dark lochs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: One tale recounts a boy who touched a Kelpie and escaped by slicing off his stuck finger.

name: Cu Chulainn
visual_anchor: Fierce young Celtic champion standing in a war chariot brandishing the barbed spear Gae Bulg, hair standing on end in a terrifying battle frenzy.
core_traits: Greatest demigod warrior hero of Irish Celtic mythology and protagonist of the Ulster Cycle
Originally named Setanta; earned his name by killing the vicious guard hound of Culann and taking its place
Wielded the deadly barbed spear Gae Bulg, which opened thirty barbs inside an enemy's flesh
Underwent the terrifying 'warp spasm' (riastrad) in combat, transforming into an unrecognizable grotesque berserker

facts_and_myths.claim: Cu Chulainn tied himself upright to a standing pillar stone with his own belt so he could die on his feet facing enemies.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mortally wounded at the Pillar Stone of Clochafarmore, he stood tall; enemies only approached after a raven landed on his shoulder.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A famous bronze statue of his death stands in the General Post Office in Dublin.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cu Chulainn was an English knight serving at King Arthur's Round Table.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cu Chulainn is strictly an Irish Gaelic warrior hero from the prehistoric Iron Age Ulster tales.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: He single-handedly defended Ulster against Queen Maeve of Connacht in the Cattle Raid of Cooley.

name: Gilgamesh
visual_anchor: Imposing Mesopotamian monarch with braided beard and gold armband holding a lion cub under his arm, standing atop the sunbaked brick walls of Uruk.
core_traits: Demigod king of Uruk and legendary hero of the ancient Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh
Two-thirds divine and one-third human, possessing peerless physical strength and courage
Formed an unbreakable bond of brotherhood with the wild man Enkidu
Slew the terrifying cedar forest monster Humbaba and the celestial Bull of Heaven
Embarked on a desperate quest to the ends of the earth to discover the secret of immortality

facts_and_myths.claim: The Epic of Gilgamesh contains an ancient Mesopotamian Great Flood narrative closely mirroring the story of Noah's Ark.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The immortal survivor Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh how he built a giant boat lined with pitch to survive the gods' apocalyptic flood.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Epic of Gilgamesh, carved on clay cuneiform tablets, is widely considered humanity's earliest surviving literary masterpiece.

facts_and_myths.claim: Gilgamesh successfully achieved physical immortality and lives forever on earth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A water serpent stole the rejuvenation plant while Gilgamesh was bathing, teaching him that mortality is mankind's universal destiny.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The serpent shed its old skin immediately after eating the plant.

name: Enkidu
visual_anchor: Muscular primitive wild man with long tangled hair and horns, running alongside gazelles and lions across the ancient Sumerian steppe.
core_traits: Wild man created from clay and saliva by the goddess Aruru to rival and humble King Gilgamesh
Lived naked among wild beasts, grazing on grass and drinking at watering holes
Civilized by the sacred temple priestess Shamhat over seven days and nights
Wrestled Gilgamesh in Uruk; their drawn battle forged a legendary lifelong brotherhood

facts_and_myths.claim: Animals fled from Enkidu once he had been civilized and introduced to human culture by Shamhat.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When Enkidu tried to return to the gazelles, they bolted in fear because he now smelled of humanity and possessed intellect.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: He taught Gilgamesh humility and empathy.

facts_and_myths.claim: Enkidu survived Gilgamesh and ruled Uruk for two centuries.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The gods struck Enkidu down with a lingering illness as punishment for killing the Bull of Heaven; his death sent Gilgamesh into grief.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Gilgamesh refused to bury Enkidu until a maggot fell from his nose.

name: Baba Yaga
visual_anchor: Fierce hooked-nosed crone flying through a birch forest inside a giant wooden mortar, steering with a pestle, heading toward a hut standing on dancing chicken legs.
core_traits: Iconic witch of Slavic folklore dwelling in the deepest part of the ancient forest
Flies through the skies seated in a giant wooden mortar, steering with a pestle and sweeping away tracks with a silver broom
Lives in a magical wooden hut that stands and spins on giant chicken legs, surrounded by a fence of human bones
Ambiguous nature: may devour children or serve as a wise, cryptic donor providing magical items to clever heroes

facts_and_myths.claim: Baba Yaga's hut is described as having no doors or windows until a hero chants: 'Hut, turn your back to the forest and face me!'
facts_and_myths.explanation: The hut spins on its chicken legs and only grants entrance when the correct traditional incantation is spoken aloud.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Her fence is made of human bones topped with glowing human skulls whose eye sockets shine light in the dark.

facts_and_myths.claim: Baba Yaga rides a conventional broomstick like Western European Halloween witches.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Baba Yaga flies inside an iron or wooden mortar (stupa), using a heavy pestle as an oar and a broom solely to sweep away her tracks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Her servant horsemen represent the White Day, Red Sun, and Black Night.

name: Koschei the Deathless
visual_anchor: Gaunt, skeletal sorcerer king wearing a spiked iron crown and flowing tattered cape, clutching a glowing crystal containing a hidden needle in an icy fortress.
core_traits: Archetypal villainous sorcerer of Slavic folklore who cannot be killed by conventional means
Hid his immortal soul outside his physical body inside a nesting puzzle of objects
His soul is in a needle, inside an egg, inside a duck, inside a hare, inside an iron chest buried under a green oak on Buyan Island
Captures beautiful maidens and princesses, including the wives of heroes like Prince Ivan

facts_and_myths.claim: Koschei dies instantly the moment the hidden magical needle containing his soul is snapped in half.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While touching the egg weakens him, snapping the tip of the needle destroys his soul, causing Koschei to perish on the spot.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This Slavic folk motif inspired the modern fantasy concept of a Lich and Voldemort's Horcruxes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Koschei was a peaceful forest monk who cured sick animals.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Koschei was a cruel, tyrannical necromancer who kidnapped princesses and turned entire armies to stone.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Prince Ivan defeated him with the aid of animals he had previously shown mercy to.

name: Kraken
visual_anchor: Colossal monstrous squid with titanic tentacle suckers wrapping around the wooden masts of a three-masted sailing ship, dragging it beneath churning waves.
core_traits: Colossal legendary marine monster of Scandinavian and Nordic folklore
Depicted as a gargantuan octopus or giant squid lurking off the coasts of Norway and Greenland
Capable of wrapping titanic tentacles around entire sailing galleons to drag them to the ocean floor
Created immense swirling whirlpools when submerging that sucked ships down into the abyss

facts_and_myths.claim: Kraken legends were almost certainly inspired by real-world encounters with giant squids (Architeuthis dux).
facts_and_myths.explanation: Giant squids reaching up to 13 meters (43 feet) with dinner-plate-sized eyes washed ashore in Scandinavia, validating sailors' tales.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Swedish bishop Olaus Magnus and Erik Pontoppidan described the Kraken as resembling an island that sailors mistook for dry land.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Kraken was a Greek monster sent by Poseidon to fight Perseus in classical Greek mythology.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The monster Perseus fought was the Greek sea beast Cetus; the Kraken was inserted into Greek myth by Hollywood's Clash of the Titans.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Alfred, Lord Tennyson wrote a famous sonnet describing the Kraken sleeping in the deep sea.

name: Leviathan
visual_anchor: Titanic armored sea monster with glowing abyssal scales, ridges of armor, and eyes shining like dawn, breaching violently through stormy waves.
core_traits: Primordial gigantic sea monster appearing in biblical mythology and ancient Near Eastern lore
Described in the Book of Job as an untameable ocean titan with impenetrable armored scales and fiery breath
Forms a cosmic trio of primordial beasts alongside Behemoth (land) and Ziz (sky)
Symbol of primordial chaos, untamed wilderness, and supreme aquatic power

facts_and_myths.claim: Philosopher Thomas Hobbes titled his famous 1651 political treatise 'Leviathan', comparing the state to a colossal sea monster.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hobbes used the biblical Leviathan as a metaphor for the absolute, all-powerful commonwealth needed to preserve social order.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An extinct prehistoric sperm whale discovered in 2008 was named Livyatan melvillei in honor of Leviathan and Herman Melville.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Leviathan was a small harmless freshwater fish that lived in the Sea of Galilee.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Leviathan was portrayed as a colossal, terrifying monster of the open ocean that laughed at spears and arrows.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Canaanite mythology, the storm god Baal slew the seven-headed sea dragon Lotan, the precursor to Leviathan.

name: Loch Ness Monster
visual_anchor: Enigmatic aquatic creature with long slender neck and humped back emerging briefly above the dark, reflective peaty waters of Loch Ness beneath ruined Urquhart Castle.
core_traits: World-famous cryptid purported to inhabit the deep, peaty waters of Loch Ness in the Scottish Highlands
Commonly described as resembling a surviving prehistoric marine reptile, such as a plesiosaur
Modern interest surged in 1933 following road construction and the famous 'Surgeon's Photograph'
Earliest recorded account dates back to 565 AD when Saint Columba commanded a water beast to retreat

facts_and_myths.claim: The iconic 1934 'Surgeon's Photograph' showing Nessie's neck was revealed to be a hoax using a toy submarine.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1994, conspirator Christian Spurling confessed that the photo showed a modified toy submarine with a plastic wood head.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A 2019 comprehensive environmental DNA survey of Loch Ness found abundant European eel DNA, suggesting giant eels might explain sightings.

facts_and_myths.claim: A living breeding population of giant reptiles has been confirmed by Scottish marine biologists.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Extensive sonar sweeps, satellite imaging, and DNA sampling have yielded zero scientific evidence of large prehistoric creatures.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Nessie generates over GBP 40 million annually for the Scottish tourism economy.

name: Bigfoot
visual_anchor: Towering ape-like biped covered in dark reddish-brown fur, taking a mid-stride glance over its shoulder through dense Pacific Northwest redwood forest.
core_traits: Legendary ape-like cryptid said to inhabit the remote forests of North America, especially the Pacific Northwest
Described as standing 7 to 9 feet tall, covered in dark brown or black fur, with massive footprint impressions
Roots lie in indigenous Salish oral traditions of the 'Sasq'ets' (wild hairy man)
Immortalized by the famous 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film clip showing a female Bigfoot walking along Bluff Creek

facts_and_myths.claim: The name 'Sasquatch' comes from the Halkomelem language of the indigenous Coast Salish people.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The word 'sasq'ets' translates to 'wild hairy man', anglicized by government agent J.W. Burns in the 1920s.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Patterson-Gimlin film's subject was nicknamed 'Patty' by cryptozoology researchers.

facts_and_myths.claim: The FBI officially classified Bigfoot as an endangered primate species in 1976.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The FBI examined 15 mystery hairs in 1976 and concluded they were deer hair; no official primate classification was made.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Washington State has an official law designating Bigfoot as an endangered species to deter hunters with firearms.

name: Yeti
visual_anchor: Massive bipedal ape-like creature with thick shaggy white-and-gray fur standing on a windswept icy Himalayan ridge against Mount Everest.
core_traits: Ape-like legendary entity of Himalayan folklore inhabiting the high snowbound peaks of Nepal, Bhutan, and Tibet
Ingrained in Sherpa and Tibetan Buddhist cultural traditions as a nocturnal wild creature
Western popular culture rebranded the creature as the 'Abominable Snowman' following 1920s Everest expeditions
Often sighted in the form of colossal mystery footprints pressed into high-altitude snowfields

facts_and_myths.claim: DNA testing of alleged Yeti relics from Himalayan monasteries revealed they belong to Himalayan brown and Asian black bears.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A comprehensive 2017 genetic study of bone, tooth, skin, and hair relics proved they came from endangered bear species.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The phrase 'Abominable Snowman' arose in 1921 when journalist Henry Newman mistranslated the Tibetan term 'Metoh-Kangmi'.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sir Edmund Hillary proved the existence of the Yeti during his 1960 Himalayan expedition.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hillary led an expedition specifically to investigate the Yeti and concluded the evidence was based on folklore and bear relics.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Himalayan monastery of Khumjung still preserves an alleged 'Yeti scalp' made of serow goat-antelope hide.

name: Werewolf
visual_anchor: Muscular, ravenous half-man half-wolf hybrid howling at a bright full moon with dripping fangs in a dark misty pine forest.
core_traits: Mythological human capable of shapeshifting into a ferocious wolf or lupine beast
Transformation is traditionally triggered by the appearance of the full moon or a curse
Transmitted through a bite or scratch from an existing werewolf
Possesses superhuman strength, speed, regenerative healing, and animal senses
Vulnerable primarily to weapons fashioned from pure solid silver

facts_and_myths.claim: The idea that werewolves are exclusively vulnerable to silver bullets was popularized largely by Hollywood cinema.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While silver was associated with the moon, the 'silver bullet' rule became a universal staple through the 1941 film The Wolf Man.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ancient Greek King Lycaon was transformed into a wolf by Zeus for serving him roasted human flesh.

facts_and_myths.claim: Medical cases of clinical lycanthropy involve actual genetic mutation turning skin into real wolf fur.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Clinical lycanthropy is a rare psychiatric delusion where a patient falsely believes they are transforming into an animal.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The medical condition hypertrichosis (werewolf syndrome) causes excessive hair growth all over the face and body.

name: Vampire
visual_anchor: Aristocratic pale nobleman clad in an ebony cape with high collar, showing razor fangs and hypnotic red eyes inside a Gothic castle.
core_traits: Immortal undead folklore creature surviving by drinking the vital blood of living humans
Nocturnal predator sleeping in native earth inside a coffin during daylight hours
Lacks a reflection in mirrors, casts no shadow, and can shapeshift into a bat, wolf, or mist
Vulnerable to direct sunlight, wooden stakes through the heart, garlic, holy water, and crucifixes

facts_and_myths.claim: Bram Stoker based aspects of Count Dracula on the historical 15th-century Wallachian prince Vlad the Impaler (Vlad Tepes).
facts_and_myths.explanation: Vlad III's patronymic Dracula ('Son of the Dragon') and his brutal reputation inspired Stoker's naming of the titular count.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word 'vampire' entered the English language in 1732 following mass vampire panics in Serbia and Austria.

facts_and_myths.claim: In original Eastern European folklore, vampires were always elegant, charming noblemen in black tuxedos.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Traditional folklore described vampires as bloated, ruddy-faced peasants in soiled shrouds; the aristocratic tuxedo was created by 19th-century theater.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Archaeologists have excavated hundreds of European 'vampire burials' pinned down with sickles or stones in mouths.

name: Frankenstein Monster
visual_anchor: Colossal stitched-together humanoid with pale green skin, dark sunken eyes, and surgical scars, standing before electrical sparks in a gothic laboratory.
core_traits: Sentient humanoid creature constructed from dead body parts by scientist Victor Frankenstein
Brought to life through galvanic electricity and scientific alchemy in Mary Shelley's 1818 masterpiece
Possesses superhuman physical strength, endurance, and remarkable intellectual eloquence
Abandoned by his creator, driven to vengeance after humanity rejects him for his terrifying appearance

facts_and_myths.claim: In Mary Shelley's original novel, the monster is nameless and never referred to as 'Frankenstein'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Victor Frankenstein is the scientist; the creature refers to himself as 'the creature', 'monster', or 'the fallen angel'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In the novel, the creature is highly articulate, reading Paradise Lost and speaking eloquent French.

facts_and_myths.claim: The creature had bolts through his neck in Mary Shelley's 1818 novel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The neck bolts and flat top head were invented in 1931 by makeup artist Jack Pierce for Boris Karloff's Universal film.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mary Shelley wrote the novel at age 18 during the famous rainy 'Year Without a Summer' at Lake Geneva.

name: Mummy
visual_anchor: Ancient embalmed corpse wrapped in weathered linen bandages stepping slowly out of an ornate gilded sarcophagus in a torchlit stone tomb.
core_traits: Deceased body preserved through artificial chemical embalming, linen wrapping, and dry desert air
Popularized in gothic horror as a vengeful reanimated corpse stalking those who desecrate royal tombs
Associated with the supernatural 'Curse of the Pharaohs' afflicting excavators
Shambles slowly with stiff linen-bound limbs, possessing supernatural strength and immunity to pain

facts_and_myths.claim: The 'Curse of the Pharaohs' media craze exploded in 1923 after Lord Carnarvon died shortly after opening King Tutankhamun's tomb.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Carnarvon died from an infected mosquito bite, which newspapers sensationalized as a deadly ancient curse.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Archaeologist Howard Carter, who actually opened the tomb, lived to age 64 and died of natural causes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ancient Egyptian mummification removed the heart and threw it away.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The heart was carefully left inside the chest because it was needed for the Weighing of the Heart judgment; the brain was extracted and discarded.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Victorian aristocrats held morbid 'mummy unwrapping parties' in 19th-century London parlors.

name: Golem
visual_anchor: Colossal faceless humanoid sculpted from river clay and mud, with the glowing Hebrew word 'EMET' carved into its forehead, standing protectively in an old synagogue.
core_traits: Anthropomorphic animated being created entirely from inanimate matter (usually river clay or mud) in Jewish folklore
Most famous legend features Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel creating the Golem of Prague in the 16th century
Created to protect the Jewish community of Prague from anti-Semitic violence and blood libel pogroms
Animated by inscribing the Hebrew word 'EMET' (Truth) on its forehead or placing a sacred parchment (shem) in its mouth

facts_and_myths.claim: The Golem is deactivated by erasing the first letter 'Aleph' from 'EMET' (Truth) on its forehead, leaving 'MET' (Dead).
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Hebrew, removing the letter Aleph transforms 'emet' (life/truth) into 'met' (death), returning the Golem to lifeless dust.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Legend says the clay remains of the Golem of Prague are still stored in the attic of the Old-New Synagogue in Prague.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Golem had the power of beautiful speech and became a famous Jewish cantor.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A Golem is completely mute; only God can grant the power of human speech and a divine soul (neshama).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word 'golem' appears once in the Bible (Psalm 139:16) meaning 'unformed substance'.

name: Djinn
visual_anchor: Majestic glowing supernatural entity swirling out from the spout of an ancient brass oil lamp in billowing blue and golden smoke.
core_traits: Supernatural spiritual beings in Islamic theology and pre-Islamic Arabian mythology
Created by God from a smokeless flame (marijin min nar) and granted free will alongside mankind
Divided into various tribes and ranks, including the powerful Ifrit and Marid
Immortalized in One Thousand and One Nights (Arabian Nights) as wish-granting spirits bound to lamps and rings

facts_and_myths.claim: According to the Quran, King Solomon possessed a magical ring (Seal of Solomon) that gave him command over all Djinn.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Solomon commanded armies of birds, men, and Djinn, employing them to build monuments and dive for ocean pearls.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word 'genie' entered English through the French translation of 'djinn' in Antoine Galland's Arabian Nights.

facts_and_myths.claim: All Djinn are benevolent blue giants that grant three wishes and sing musical numbers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In authentic Arabian lore, Djinn possess moral agency and can be good, evil, or neutral, often mischievous or dangerous.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The English word 'genius' is etymologically distinct, deriving from Latin genius (guardian spirit).

name: Basilisk
visual_anchor: Sinister crested serpentine beast with glowing yellow eyes slithering across scorched stone, leaving withered grass and cracked rocks in its wake.
core_traits: Legendary reptile hailed in European bestiaries as the 'King of Serpents'
Possesses a gaze so lethal that looking directly into its eyes causes instantaneous death
Breathes venomous fumes so toxic that it withers vegetation and shatters rocks
Vulnerable only to its own reflection in a mirror, the scent of a weasel, or the crowing of a rooster

facts_and_myths.claim: Pliny the Elder recorded in the 1st century that the weasel is the only animal immune to the Basilisk's deadly venom.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pliny wrote that weasels hunt basilisks by eating wild rue beforehand to neutralize the poison.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The modern Central American Basilisk lizard is named after it and nicknamed the 'Jesus Christ lizard' for running on water.

facts_and_myths.claim: The crowing of a rooster was believed to cause a Basilisk to instantly die.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Medieval travelers often carried roosters on journeys through unknown lands to protect against encountering a Basilisk.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bestiaries claimed it hatched from a toad or snake incubating an egg laid by a rooster.

name: Wendigo
visual_anchor: Emaciated skeletal monster with decaying gray skin, glowing hollow eyes, and deer antlers lurking behind frozen pine trees in a howling sub-zero blizzard.
core_traits: Malevolent supernatural creature and spirit in the oral mythology of the indigenous Algonquian peoples
Associated with winter, famine, starvation, and the taboo of human cannibalism
Humans who resort to eating human flesh in winter are believed to transform into a ravenous Wendigo
Cursed with an insatiable hunger; every time it eats a victim, it grows in size and becomes hungrier

facts_and_myths.claim: The psychological term 'Wendigo psychosis' describes a rare culture-bound syndrome involving intense craving for human flesh.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Historically observed among northern indigenous hunters during isolated, starving winters.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The deer-skull and antler aesthetic was popularized by modern horror cinema; original folklore described an emaciated, frostbitten human form.

facts_and_myths.claim: A Wendigo can be easily killed by offering it sweet honey cakes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Folklore states a Wendigo possesses an icy heart that must be pierced with silver or completely melted with fire to be destroyed.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its icy breath was said to carry the scent of rotting meat.

name: Flying Dutchman
visual_anchor: Spectral glowing ghost ship with tattered sails and luminous green hull sailing against violent gale-force winds through stormy midnight seas off Cape Horn.
core_traits: Legendary ghost ship condemned to sail the high seas forever, unable to make port
Haunts the treacherous, stormy waters around the Cape of Good Hope at the southern tip of Africa
Commanded by Captain Hendrick van der Decken, who swore an arrogant blasphemous oath to round the Cape even if it took till Doomsday
Regarded by mariners as a terrifying omen of imminent shipwreck, doom, and disaster

facts_and_myths.claim: In 1881, the future King George V of Britain recorded sighting the phantom ship Flying Dutchman from HMS Bacchante.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Prince George's personal log recorded thirteen officers and men witnessing a spectral red-glowing ship pass across their bow.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The lookout who first reported the ship fell from the topmast to his death the following day.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sightings of the Flying Dutchman are often scientific optical illusions known as superior mirages (Fata Morgana).
facts_and_myths.explanation: Atmospheric temperature inversions refract light over cold waters, causing real ships beyond the horizon to appear floating in mid-air.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Richard Wagner composed the famous 1843 romantic opera Der fliegende Hollander based on the legend.
